core: The World Wide Web is a service that runs on top of the internet, not the internet itself
The client-server model: a browser (client) requests resources; a web server hosts and sends them
Web pages are built from files, chiefly HTML (structure), with CSS (style) and JavaScript (behavior)
A URL is the address of a resource, made of a scheme, host/domain, and path (plus optional port, query, fragment)
DNS translates a human-readable domain name into the numeric IP address of a server
The HTTP/HTTPS request-response cycle: the browser sends a request, the server returns a response
HTTPS adds TLS encryption so the request and response cannot be read or altered in transit
The round trip to load a page: DNS lookup, TCP connection, HTTP request, response, render
supporting: HTTP is a stateless application-layer protocol that runs over TCP (and TLS for HTTPS)
A domain name is read right to left: top-level domain, then labels/subdomains
Status codes such as 200 signal the outcome of a request
A response is delivered as packets that the browser reassembles and renders
outOfScope: IP addressing, packets, routers, and the TCP/IP stack as infrastructure (owned by Internet Basics)
The browser application's features, tabs, extensions, and settings (owned by Browsers)
How search engines crawl and rank pages (owned by Search Engines)
Email protocols such as SMTP/IMAP (owned by Email Basics)

claims.claim: The internet is the physical/network infrastructure, while the Web is a service built on top of it; the two are not the same thing.
The Web follows a client-server model: the client is the user's internet-connected device and browser; the server is a computer that stores web pages and sends a copy to the client on request.
A URL is the address of a unique resource on the Web, composed of a scheme (protocol), an authority (host/domain and optional port), and a path, with optional query and fragment parts.
DNS translates a human-readable domain name into the numeric IP address of the server hosting the site, acting like a directory so people do not have to memorize IP addresses.
HTTP is a stateless, application-level request/response protocol; the browser sends a request identifying a resource and the server returns a response with a status code and the resource's data.
HTTPS is HTTP carried over a TLS-encrypted connection, so the exchange is protected from being read or tampered with in transit.

Loading a page involves a round trip: DNS lookup to find the IP address, a TCP connection to the server, an HTTP request, the server's response, and the browser rendering the returned HTML/CSS/JavaScript.
Web pages are written primarily in HTML for structure, with CSS for presentation and JavaScript for interactivity; the browser assembles these files into the displayed page.

sourceRecords.title: How the web works
sourceRecords.notes: Defines clients (user devices + browser) and servers (computers that store pages and send a copy on request); lists the page-load steps (DNS lookup, HTTP request over TCP/IP, 200 OK response, packets reassembled and rendered) and the HTML/CSS/JavaScript roles. Facts restated in original prose.

sourceRecords.title: What is a URL?
sourceRecords.notes: URL as the address of a unique resource; parts are scheme (e.g. https), authority (host/domain + optional port such as 443), path, and optional query (?q=...) and fragment (#...). Fragment is not sent to the server. Used to support the URL-anatomy section.

sourceRecords.title: What is a domain name?
sourceRecords.notes: Domain names are human-readable stand-ins for IP addresses, read right to left (TLD then labels/SLD/subdomains). Describes the DNS lookup flow: browser checks local cache, otherwise queries a DNS server that returns the IP address, then the browser connects to the server. Supports the DNS section.

sourceRecords.title: An overview of HTTP
sourceRecords.notes: HTTP is a client-server protocol for fetching resources, layered on TCP (network layer IP); requests carry a method, path, version, headers and optional body; responses carry a version, status code/message, headers and optional body. HTTPS = HTTP over a TLS-encrypted TCP connection. HTTP is stateless. Supports HTTP/HTTPS sections.

sourceRecords.title: How does the Internet work?
sourceRecords.notes: States that the Internet is infrastructure while the Web is a service built on top of it. Used only for the internet-vs-web distinction; infrastructure detail (routers, ISPs, IP) kept as reference and out of scope for this lesson.

sourceRecords.title: RFC 9110: HTTP Semantics
sourceRecords.notes: Authoritative definition: HTTP is a family of stateless, application-level request/response protocols; clients send request messages toward an identified origin server, which responds; resources are identified by URIs using http or https schemes. Used to anchor the HTTP definition and client-server model.

sourceRecords.title: Domain Name System (DNS) - ICANN Acronyms and Terms
sourceRecords.notes: ICANN describes DNS as the system that lets a familiar domain name be used instead of a hard-to-remember IP address, comparing an IP address to a telephone number. Read via curl with a browser user-agent (WebFetch returned 403). Supports the 'phone book' framing of DNS.
